topic: Combination padlock: why you spin the dial 3 times first. A drive pin on the dial picks up wheel 1, its pin picks up wheel 2, then wheel 3; then each number sets one wheel's notch under the latch
title: Why You Spin a Combination Lock 3 Times 🔒
principle: A single-dial combination lock has a stack of loose wheels on one axis, each with a notch (gate); the dial turns a drive cam whose pin can only catch a small fly on the nearest wheel after nearly a full turn, and each wheel's own pin catches the next wheel the same way, so it takes one turn per wheel to pick them all up; you then stop at the first number (the wheel furthest from the dial is set), reverse so the pins let go of it and pick up the others again to set the second, reverse again for the last, and when all the gates line up under the fence the latch drops into them and releases the shackle.
caption:
Why You Spin a Combination Lock 3 Times 🔒
Guess: which wheel do you set first, front or back? 👇

firstComment:
Answer: the back wheel 🔧

Behind the dial sits a stack of loose wheels on one axle, one wheel for each number, and each wheel has a notch. A latch rests on the wheels' rims and can only drop when all the notches line up under it.

The dial turns a drive cam with a small pin. The pin can only catch a tab on the first wheel after almost a full turn. That wheel has its own pin, which catches the second wheel a turn later, and so on. So with three wheels it takes about three turns to pick them all up. That's why you spin it first.

Stop at the first number: the wheel furthest from the dial is now in place. Turn the other way: the pins let go of it, so it stays put, and they pick up the other wheels again to set the second number. Turn back for the last number. When every notch lines up, the latch drops in and the lock opens.

(Simplified 3D model of a three-wheel dial lock. The exact number of turns and the direction of each step depend on the brand and model, so always follow your lock's own instructions.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Rotary combination lock (wheels with notches called gates; the dial's spindle turns a cam with a drive pin that engages a fly on the closest wheel; each wheel's drive pin engages the next wheel; once all wheels are picked up, the first number sets the wheel furthest from the cam; reversing leaves it in place; when the gates align, the fence drops into them): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotary_combination_lock
HowStuffWorks, How Combination Locks Work (one wheel for each number; the drive pin spins the first wheel until it contacts the next, which is called picking up the wheels; when the notches line up they form a gap): https://home.howstuffworks.com/home-improvement/household-safety/security/combination-lock.htm
Wikipedia, Combination lock (single-dial locks are opened by turning the dial clockwise to the first number, counterclockwise to the second, and so on; when the notches align, the latch fits into them and the lock opens): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combination_lock

voiceover: Why do you spin a combination lock three times first?
Behind the dial hide three loose wheels. Each one has a notch.
A latch rests on top. It can only drop when all three notches line up.
Turn right. A pin on the dial catches wheel one.
Wheel one's pin catches wheel two. Then wheel two catches wheel three.
Three spins, three wheels picked up.
Stop at the first number. The back wheel's notch is now under the latch.
Turn left two turns. The back wheel stays put, and the pins pick up the other two.
Stop at the second number. The middle notch lines up.
Turn right to the last number. The front notch lines up.
All three notches line up. The latch drops in, and the lock opens!
Each spin picks up one more wheel.
